newsitem.title: USA: U.S. campaign funds uproar a big Clinton headache.
newsitem.headline: U.S. campaign funds uproar a big Clinton headache.

text.p: Is the White House for sale, or at least for rent, to donors of big-time political cash?

A stack of memos and notes to and from President Bill Clinton and some of his political advisers, released Tuesday in a White House candor campaign, have made that one central question in a campaign fund-raising uproar that has grown steadily worse since Clinton's re-election last November.
It has the Democratic president himself on the hot seat.

The new centre of attention -- in front-page newspaper leads accompanied by photographed copies -- is a 1995 note to top political aides in Clinton's handwriting instructing them to invite top campaign donors, including those who have given $50,000 or $100,000 or more, to meet him over lunch, coffee or other events in the White House. The elite would even get to spend the night, and that should start "right away."

This was in 1995 when the Democrats were coming off a stunning election loss that gave control of Congress to the Republicans. Party strategists told Clinton they needed dramatic ways to "energize" backers for the next battle.

These revelations forced Clinton and top aides to deny they used entree to a hallowed American shrine as bait for campaign money. That added to a broader influence-peddling issue of whether Democrats had raised millions illegally by soliciting funds from foreign interests.
Many analysts say the latter question is the more serious one for the integrity of American politics and government. But the White House entree question may stir more public outrage.

It forced the president into a long, defensive explanation to reporters as to why the invitations were being misconstrued and were perfectly legal, even proper, expressions of gratitude to people he was "proud" to call his friends.

He ended with a much-quoted line that may enter American political lexicon: "The Lincoln Bedroom was never sold." This was a reference to a White House bedroom once used as Abraham Lincoln's office and where he signed the Emancipation Proclamation freeing the slaves.

His explanations failed to stem a tide of unflattering lead-story television and newspaper publicity -- and the din is likely to get louder in coming weeks and months, as two congressional committees controlled by Republicans gear up for hearings. Among other things, they will want to know whether U.S. foreign policy decisions were swayed by big contributors or if businesses won special consideration from government.

Besides the congressional probes, the Justice Department has a task force of 25 FBI agents investigating possible crimes involving donations for the 1996 elections -- the most expensive ever with some $2.7 billion raised by Democrats and Republicans for presidential and congressional elections.

The new White House-access flap only underscores what Democrats consider a bitterly unfair turn in the fund-raising controversy: Republicans actually raised more of the campaign cash in question and have questions to answer themselves.
But Clinton is president, and most of the examples of questionable recent fund-raising have involved his party.

The accumulating controversy has stirred a rising chorus of calls for appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate campaign financing questions. Attorney General Janet Reno has rejected such requests, arguing her Justice Department could handle the matter itself. But it is led by Clinton appointees and her position may be hard to maintain.

Former senior White House adviser George Stephanopoulos, one of Clinton's top confidants, conceded as much in an ABC News interview on Wednesday and said the controversy would probably haunt Clinton for some time to come.
"This is going to be a lot of trouble over this year for the president," he said.
He also offered a summary of the White House defence that everyone is guilty of similar campaign fund-raising excesses because the American system forces it and needs reform.

"People gave money in the hopes they would see the president. And they did," he said. "People gave money to the Republican congressmen in the hopes they would block tobacco legislation or gut the endangered species act or weaken the clean water act. It happens all the time. It is horrible. The system stinks. It has to be changed."

Most of the finance controversy has concerned donations from Democratic backers with business ties to Indonesia, Thailand, South Korean, Vietnam, Taiwan, India, China, Paraguay and Russia as well as White House visitors who included a Chinese arms dealer and convicted drug dealer.

It is illegal for non-citizens or foreign firms to give to campaigns unless nationals are legal U.S. residents. American corporations or subsidiaries of foreign firms doing substantial U.S. business can donate to political parties for general party-building purposes, however.

Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Arlen Specter, one of the Senate committee investigators, said Wednesday: "The issue of the Lincoln bedroom is tantalizing but not nearly as important as the illegal contributions which were made by foreigners and the time sequence where major changes were made in foreign policy. That is illegal now and has to be investigated."
Clinton says donations never affected his policy decisions or bought White House access. He admits "mistakes were made."
